Predicting Hotel Booking Cancellations — a CRISP-DM Project¶

Author: Meron Tesfandrias · Course: CMPE 255 · Repo: MeronDT/CMPE-255-Data-Mining-process · App: <deployed URL>

Data: Hotel booking demand datasets — N. António, A. de Almeida & L. Nunes, Data in Brief 22 (2019) 41–49, doi:10.1016/j.dib.2018.11.126. 119,390 bookings for a resort hotel (H1) and a city hotel (H2) in Portugal, arrivals July 2015 – August 2017. Mirrored on Kaggle as jessemostipak/hotel-booking-demand and in the TidyTuesday repo (used here — no login needed).

This notebook follows the CRISP-DM 1.0 reference model end to end: each phase is broken into its generic tasks, and each task produces the outputs CRISP-DM defines for it.

# Phase Generic tasks
1 Business Understanding Determine business objectives · Assess situation · Determine data mining goals · Produce project plan
2 Data Understanding Collect initial data · Describe data · Explore data · Verify data quality
3 Data Preparation Select · Clean · Construct · Integrate · Format data
4 Modeling Select modeling technique · Generate test design · Build model · Assess model
5 Evaluation Evaluate results · Review process · Determine next steps
6 Deployment Plan deployment · Plan monitoring & maintenance · Produce final report · Review project

Headline result. A calibrated random-forest model that estimates each booking's cancellation probability from the 24 fields known when it is booked.

  • What it is used for. For each arrival date, the probabilities are added up into an expected number of cancellations, which tells the hotel how many extra rooms to sell.
  • The business case. On the most recent 20 % of arrivals, which were never used for training or tuning, this per-night forecast misses the true number of cancellations by 4.6 rooms on average. The hotel's current rule of thumb misses by 9.4. Under the assumed costs it is worth €3,400 more per 1,000 bookings than that rule (95 % CI €2,400–€4,300).
  • What it is not good at. As a per-booking classifier it misses two of its three data mining targets: ROC-AUC is 0.827 (target 0.85) and recall at the cost-optimal threshold is 0.47 (target 0.50). Precision is 0.83 (target 0.75). So it is approved for the overbooking forecast, not for acting on individual bookings.
  • What changed it. The most predictive field, guest nationality, was excluded. A test in the data showed it was probably filled in by default for guests who never arrived, which leaks the outcome.

It is deployed as a Streamlit app that reads raw booking-system fields. (The test period was scored once in the first iteration and was visible during the later review rounds; see 4.2.)

How to run: Runtime → Run all (≈ 7–10 min on free Colab). All figures, reports, the model and the app are written to artifacts/.

CV_FOLDS     = 5
N_TUNING_ITER = 8              # random-search iterations per model family (the same budget for every family)

# Phase 1.3 data mining success criteria. ROC-AUC and precision were fixed before modeling; the recall floor was
# added in revision 2 (critiques/round_2.md) because precision alone can be met by raising the threshold.
SUCCESS_CRITERIA = {"roc_auc": 0.85, "precision": 0.75, "recall": 0.50}

# Phase 1.2 cost/benefit assumptions. The model's ONE action is internal: rooms are added to a night's overbooking
# allowance (guests are never contacted, so nationality never drives a guest-facing action). Both outcomes depend on
# the same event - the hotel filling up that night - so both are weighted by P_FULL (revision 3).
P_FULL       = 0.5      # share of nights on which demand would fill the hotel (assumed; to confirm with the hotel)
RESALE_VALUE = 100.0    # a freed room re-sold on a full night (about one night's ADR)
WALK_COST    = 200.0    # walking a guest on a full night: room elsewhere, transport, compensation (~2 nights' ADR)
VALUE_TP = RESALE_VALUE * P_FULL   # expected value of a correct flag  = EUR 50
COST_FP  = WALK_COST * P_FULL      # expected cost of a wrong flag     = EUR 100
COST_FN  = 0.0                     # missed cancellation = today's status quo

Phase 1 — Business Understanding¶

Goal: understand the project objectives from a business perspective, convert them into a data mining problem definition, and draw up a preliminary plan.

1.1 Determine business objectives¶

Output: Background¶

The stakeholder is the revenue-management team of two hotels in Portugal — a resort hotel in the Algarve (H1) and a city hotel in Lisbon (H2) — whose booking records were published by António, de Almeida & Nunes (2019). Across July 2015 – August 2017, 37 % of all bookings were cancelled (42 % in the city hotel). Cancellations are a structural problem in hospitality: free-cancellation policies and online travel agencies make it cheap for guests to book speculatively. A room released a few days before arrival is often impossible to re-sell. The usual defence is to overbook each night by a fixed rule of thumb (the historical cancellation rate), and that risks "walking" guests (relocating them to another hotel) when more people turn up than expected. Today, neither hotel estimates cancellation risk per booking. At roughly 55,000 bookings a year and €346 of room revenue per arrived booking (2.3), cancellations touch about €7 M of booked revenue a year across the two hotels.

Output: Business objectives¶

  • Primary objective: reduce the revenue lost to cancellations by setting each night's overbooking level from the bookings actually on the books, instead of from a fixed historical rate. The model's output is used internally only; guests are not contacted on the basis of a score.
  • Related business questions: Which booking characteristics drive cancellation? Do the city and resort hotels behave differently? Which channels and customer types are riskiest?
  • Expected benefits: more re-sold rooms and fewer walked guests than the current rule of thumb.

Output: Business success criteria¶

Criterion Measure Target Judged by
Revenue recovered net value per 1,000 bookings of the overbooking decisions, simulated per night with the cost model in 1.2 above the hotel's current rule of thumb, with the 95 % confidence interval of the difference above zero Revenue manager
Forecast accuracy average error of the nightly overbooking number (rooms per night) smaller than the current rule's error Revenue manager
Actionability share of flagged high-risk bookings that really cancel ≥ 75 % Front-office manager
Usability staff can score the day's booking file without technical help 3 reservations staff score a day's file unaided in under 5 minutes during the pilot Reservations team

Revisions 2 and 3 replaced the original benchmarks ("flag everything", then the Non Refund rule) with the incumbent rule of thumb, which is what the hotel actually does today.

1.2 Assess situation¶

Output: Inventory of resources¶

Resource Available
Personnel the analyst (author); an AI assistant (Claude) for code review and expert critique; the course instructor. No hotel stakeholder or finance contact (see risks)
Data 2 CSV files (H1 resort 40,060 rows; H2 city 79,330 rows), 31 attributes, open data
Computing Google Colab (free tier), GitHub
Software Python, pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, Streamlit; optionally IBM SPSS Modeler

Output: Requirements, assumptions and constraints¶

  • Requirements: predictions may use only information known when the booking is made; results must be explainable to hotel staff; the model must be deployable as a simple web app that accepts the hotel's own booking fields; the work must be reproducible end to end.
  • Legal and ethical requirement: nationality is personal data under GDPR, and treating guests differently by nationality would be discriminatory. The output may therefore drive only the internal overbooking level, never a guest-facing action such as a deposit request. (After 2.3, nationality is not a model input at all.)
  • Assumptions: 2015–2017 booking behaviour is representative of future bookings; the published data is accurate (hotel and customer identifiers were removed by the authors).
  • Constraints: no booking ID, no explicit booking date (it can be derived as arrival date − lead time, see 5.1), no price history, no customer history beyond two counts; public data only; free-tier compute.

Output: Risks and contingencies¶

Risk Likelihood Impact Contingency
Target leakage from fields filled in after booking High High audit each attribute for "known at booking time?" (2.4, 3.1), test suspicious fields in the data (2.3) and their effect (5.2)
No access to the business: costs, demand and recording practices are all assumed High High cost sensitivity in 5.1; validate the assumptions at a pilot kick-off before go-live
2015–17 behaviour no longer representative (pre-pandemic, before today's OTA and free-cancellation norms) High High treat this model as a proof of concept; retrain on the hotel's recent booking-system data before go-live (6.2)
Behaviour shifts over time (concept drift) Medium High time-based test split and time-series validation; drift monitoring (6.2)
Model misses the success criteria Medium Medium feature construction, tuning; revisit goals (5.3)
Data-quality quirks (e.g. odd deposit codes) Medium Medium investigate and document (2.3, 2.4)

Output: Terminology¶

Term Meaning
ADR Average Daily Rate — revenue per occupied room-night (EUR)
Lead time days between booking and arrival
No-show guest neither cancelled nor arrived (counted as a cancellation here)
Overbooking / "walking" a guest selling more rooms than exist; relocating a guest when everyone shows up
Expected cancellations the sum of the cancellation probabilities of the bookings arriving on a date
ROC-AUC probability that the model ranks a random cancellation above a random non-cancellation
Precision / recall share of flagged bookings that really cancel / share of cancellations that are flagged
Calibration whether a predicted 30 % really means that 30 % of such bookings cancel

Output: Costs and benefits¶

An arrived booking brings about €346 of room revenue (mean of ADR × nights over arrived bookings, 2.3; median €259). Both outcomes of an overbooking decision depend on the same event: the hotel filling up that night. Both are therefore weighted by the same probability P_FULL:

Outcome Business meaning Assumed value Reasoning
A room that was oversold is freed by a cancellation it is re-sold, if demand fills the hotel +€100 × 50 % = +€50 about one night's ADR (€100), on a full night
A room that was oversold is NOT freed (the guest arrives) a guest is walked, if the hotel is full −€200 × 50 % = −€100 a comparable room elsewhere, transport and compensation (about 2 nights' ADR), on a full night
Cancellation not anticipated same as today €0 the loss happens with or without the model
Booking arrives, not overbooked normal stay €0 —

A wrong call therefore costs twice what a right call earns. These are assumptions, not hotel figures, so 5.1 re-derives the threshold and the value for cost ratios from 0.5 to 4. Revision 3 applied P_FULL to both sides; revision 2 had applied it to the walk cost only.

1.3 Determine data mining goals¶

Output: Data mining goals¶

Build a binary classifier that estimates, at booking time, the probability that a booking will be cancelled (is_canceled = 1, including no-shows). One row = one booking. The probabilities must be calibrated, because they are added up into the nightly expected cancellations. Calibration is judged descriptively (reliability curve, Brier score) and through the forecast-accuracy business criterion. Secondary goal: identify the main drivers of cancellation.

Output: Data mining success criteria¶

Metric Threshold Why
ROC-AUC on the most recent 20 % of arrivals ≥ 0.85 the model must rank risky bookings well
Precision at the chosen decision threshold ≥ 0.75 3 of 4 flagged bookings must truly cancel, or staff will ignore the flags
Recall at the chosen decision threshold ≥ 0.50 at least half of all cancellations must be caught; without this floor the precision target could be met by flagging almost nothing. Added in revision 2, after the first results were known

1.4 Produce project plan¶

Output: Project plan¶

Phase Duration (planned) Resources Outputs Risks / dependencies
Business Understanding 1 day analyst, AI critic sections 1.1–1.4 —
Data Understanding 1 day Colab data description, exploration and quality reports data access
Data Preparation 1–2 days Colab modeling dataset + reports leakage decisions
Modeling 1 day Colab candidate and tuned models compute time on free tier
Evaluation 1 day analyst, AI critic approved model, business case criteria not met → iterate
Deployment 1–2 days Streamlit Cloud, GitHub app, monitoring plan, report, article, video hosting

Iterations expected: Data Preparation ↔ Modeling (feature and leakage decisions), and Evaluation → Business Understanding if the criteria are not met. Both happened, over three review rounds:

  • the test design was changed after the first evaluation (4.2);
  • the business case was rebuilt around one action (the nightly overbooking level) and the hotel's current rule as benchmark;
  • a test in the data led back from Evaluation to Data Preparation: nationality was excluded as probable leakage (2.3, 3.1).

Output: Initial assessment of tools and techniques¶

Python and scikit-learn in Colab make the whole project reproducible from one notebook. Candidate techniques: logistic regression as an interpretable benchmark; random forest and gradient boosting for non-linear effects and interactions (e.g. lead time × deposit type × market segment). Streamlit gives a free, code-based deployment. IBM SPSS Modeler would support the same CRISP-DM flow visually but adds licensing; it was not needed.

🔍 Critic review — Business Understanding¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on CRISP-DM, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on the CRISP-DM methodology. Review the Business Understanding phase of my hotel-cancellation project below. Check it against every generic task and output CRISP-DM 1.0 defines for this phase. Focus especially on: whether the business objective, business success criteria and data mining success criteria are measurable and consistent with each other, and whether the cost/benefit assumptions are realistic and justified. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Cost figures were unjustified and the false-positive cost (€40) looked too low next to the cost of walking a guest; precision target needed a rationale. Derived costs from the average booking (€358): +€100 / −€100; justified the 75 % precision target as staff trust.
2 One flag served three different actions priced alike; no recall floor; "beat flag-all" a straw man; no legal requirement on nationality; no cost sensitivity. (C+ overall) One internal action; walk cost × P(full); recall ≥ 0.50; Non Refund rule as benchmark; GDPR requirement; cost-ratio grid.
3 P(full) applied to the walk cost only; benchmark should be the hotel's current overbooking rule; no stakeholder-access risk. (B− overall) Both outcomes × P(full) → 2 : 1 ratio; business criterion = beat the current rule per night (CI > 0); new risk row.

import re

def harmonize(d, hotel):
    """Standardise one source file: snake_case names, trimmed text, 'NULL' -> missing, hotel label."""
    d = d.copy()
    d.columns = [re.sub(r"(?<!^)(?=[A-Z][a-z])", "_", c).lower() for c in d.columns]   # IsCanceled -> is_canceled, ADR -> adr
    for c in d.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns:
        d[c] = d[c].astype(str).str.strip().replace({"NULL": np.nan, "nan": np.nan, "": np.nan})
    for c in ("agent", "company", "children"):
        d[c] = pd.to_numeric(d[c], errors="coerce")
    d.insert(0, "hotel", hotel)
    return d

# Stack both hotels for exploration (formally validated in 3.4 Integrate data)

Output: Data description report¶

The integrated data has 119,390 bookings × 32 attributes (31 original + hotel): 16–17 integer, 1–2 float and 13 text fields per file. Units: money in EUR (adr), durations in days or nights.

Format problems found and fixed in harmonize(): Children is an integer in one file and a float in the other; Meal, ReservedRoomType, AssignedRoomType and DepositType are padded with spaces; Agent and Company store missing values as the text "NULL" (16,340 and 112,593 times). Column names are CamelCase in the source and are converted to snake_case.

Against the Phase 1 requirement "known at booking time", three groups emerge: clearly known at booking (lead time, dates, stay length, guests, meal, segment, channel, deposit, ADR…); only known after the outcome (reservation_status, reservation_status_date, assigned_room_type); and ambiguous (booking_changes, required_car_parking_spaces, total_of_special_requests, country), which can be updated between booking and arrival. 2.4 and 5.2 deal with these.

def rate_plot(col, order=None, top=None, ax=None):
    g = raw.groupby(col)[TARGET].agg(["mean", "size"])
    if top: g = g.sort_values("size", ascending=False).head(top)
    g = g.reindex(order) if order else g.sort_values("mean")
    g["mean"].plot.barh(ax=ax, color="#C44E52", title=f"Cancellation rate by {col}")
    for i, (m, n) in enumerate(zip(g["mean"], g["size"])):
        ax.text(m, i, f" {m:.0%} (n={n:,})", va="center", fontsize=8)
    ax.axvline(rate, ls="--", c="gray"); ax.set_xlim(0, 1.15)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 9))
rate_plot("deposit_type", ax=axes[0, 0]); rate_plot("market_segment", ax=axes[0, 1])

# Finding Hypothesis / implication Tested?
1 The city hotel cancels far more than the resort (41.7 % vs 27.8 %) include hotel; evaluate performance per hotel (5.1) yes, 5.1
2 Cancellation rises steadily with lead time: 9.6 % for bookings made ≤ 7 days ahead, 56 % at 6–12 months, 68 % beyond a year lead_time will be a key driver yes: alone it ranks cancellations with AUC 0.70 (2.4)
3 Non Refund deposits cancel 99.4 % of the time, the opposite of what a non-refundable deposit should do. The 14,587 bookings are 97 % from Portugal and 97 % Groups or offline tour-operator bookings. They have almost no special requests, a median lead time of 183 days, and 98 % of them are exact duplicate rows. They are spread over 403 arrival dates. Most likely block allocations by tour operators (many identical rooms on one contract), recorded as "non refund" and later released. Keep the attribute (it is known at booking), report it as a data-quality question for the hotel, and show results without these bookings (5.1) partly: supported by the duplicate profile; only the hotel can confirm
4 Guests from Portugal: 62 % of cancelled bookings vs 28 % of arrived ones. Test for a defaulted value (printed table, Non Refund excluded): within every market segment, bookings that never reached the front desk (cancellations and no-shows) are Portuguese far more often than checked-out ones. Groups: 97 % / 97 % vs 29 %. Offline TA/TO: 95 % / 99 % vs 24 %. Corporate: 95 % / 93 % vs 73 %. A real nationality effect would not make no-shows look like cancellations and unlike arrivals within the same segment. The pattern fits nationality being filled in by default (Portugal) unless confirmed at check-in, so country partly encodes the outcome yes: supported → country is excluded (3.1); the effect of adding it back is measured in 5.2
5 Groups (61 %) and online travel agents (37 %) cancel most; direct (15 %) and corporate (19 %) bookings least; more special requests go with fewer cancellations (rank-correlation matrix) keep market_segment, distribution_channel, total_of_special_requests yes, 5.1 drivers
6 Seasonality differs by hotel: the resort's cancellation rate ranges from 15 % (January) to 33 % (August); the city hotel stays at 37–46 % year round keep month/week; expect seasonal drift in monitoring yes, 6.2
7 Like for like, cancellations rose: April–August 2017 vs April–August 2016, the city hotel went from 39.5 % to 43.9 % and the resort from 29.5 % to 35.1 % behaviour drifts upward, so the most recent period will be harder; this motivates the time-based test split yes: the test period is harder than CV (5.1)
8 Exact duplicate rows (34 % of all rows when both copies are counted) are 36 % Non Refund. The duplicates outside Non Refund cancel at 35.5 % (like all bookings) and are 58 % Groups / offline tour-operator bookings duplicates are mostly multi-room group bookings, not data errors, so they are kept, but they must never straddle a validation fold (4.2) yes, 4.2

def leakage_suspects(df, target, max_levels=30, min_share=0.01):
    """Flag attributes where a sizeable group has a (near-)deterministic outcome — a classic sign of leakage."""
    rows = []
    for c in df.columns.drop(target):
        if df[c].nunique() > max_levels: continue
        g = df.groupby(c)[target].agg(["mean", "size"]); g = g[g["size"] >= min_share * len(df)]
        pure = g[(g["mean"] <= 0.01) | (g["mean"] >= 0.99)]
        if len(pure):
            rows.append({"attribute": c, "pure_groups": ", ".join(f"{k}→{m:.1%} (n={s:,})" for k, (m, s) in pure.iterrows())})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

suspects = leakage_suspects(raw, TARGET)
suspects.to_csv(REP / "leakage_suspects.csv", index=False)
print("\nLeakage suspects (groups with ≥99 % or ≤1 % cancellation):"); display(suspects)

# Second detector that covers EVERY attribute, including high-cardinality (country, agent) and numeric ones:
# how well does each attribute ALONE rank cancellations among later arrivals? Categories are target-encoded on
# earlier arrivals only, and the evaluation block (60th-80th percentile of arrival dates) stays out of the test period.
arrival = pd.to_datetime(raw["arrival_date_year"].astype(str) + "-" + raw["arrival_date_month"] + "-"
                         + raw["arrival_date_day_of_month"].astype(str), format="%Y-%B-%d")
fit_mask = arrival <= arrival.quantile(0.6)
eval_mask = (arrival > arrival.quantile(0.6)) & (arrival <= arrival.quantile(0.8))
def single_feature_auc(col):
    s = raw[col]
    if s.dtype.kind in "if":
        score = s[eval_mask].fillna(s[fit_mask].median())
    else:
        enc = raw.loc[fit_mask, TARGET].groupby(s[fit_mask].astype(str)).mean()
        score = s[eval_mask].astype(str).map(enc).fillna(raw.loc[fit_mask, TARGET].mean())
    auc = roc_auc_score(raw.loc[eval_mask, TARGET], score)
    return max(auc, 1 - auc)
single_auc = pd.Series({c: single_feature_auc(c) for c in raw.columns.drop(TARGET)}).round(3).sort_values(ascending=False)
single_auc.to_frame("single_attribute_auc").to_csv(REP / "leakage_single_attribute_auc.csv")
print("Single-attribute ROC-AUC on later arrivals (> 0.80 from one field alone is suspicious):")
display(single_auc.head(12).to_frame("single_attribute_auc"))

Problem Extent Remedy
reservation_status, reservation_status_date perfectly reveal the outcome (100 % / 0 % cancellation by status; reservation_status alone gives AUC 1.00) exclude (target leakage)
assigned_room_type set at check-in exclude (not known at booking time)
booking_changes accumulates after booking exclude
required_car_parking_spaces 0 cancellations among 7,416 bookings with parking → almost certainly recorded at arrival exclude; sensitivity tested in 5.2
country probably defaulted to Portugal for bookings that never reached check-in (2.3 finding 4) exclude; sensitivity tested in 5.2
total_of_special_requests, adr can be added (requests) or revised at checkout (ADR) after booking keep: on their own they reach AUC 0.61 and well below 0.70 on later arrivals; dropping ADR changes nothing (5.2)
deposit_type = Non Refund cancels 99.4 % 14,587 bookings, mostly duplicated group/tour-operator blocks keep; flagged as a question for the hotel; results reported with and without them (5.1)
company missing 94.3 % replace by a has_company flag (missing = no company)
agent missing 13.7 % category none (missing = booked without an agent)
children missing 4 bookings set to 0 (no children recorded), consistently for children, total_guests and has_kids
Exact duplicate rows 31,994 (27 %) keep: there is no booking ID, and the profile (finding 8) shows they are mostly multi-room group bookings. Validation folds are cut at date boundaries so copies never straddle a fold (4.2)
0-guest bookings, negative ADR, ADR > €1,000 180, 1, 1 drop rows
ADR = 0 outside the Complementary segment 1,279 keep: free upgrades, staff and package stays are plausible and cannot be verified
0-night bookings 715 keep (day-use rooms are legitimate)
Stays > 30 nights; > 10 adults; ≥ 9 children or babies on one booking 24; 12; 3 keep: long stays and group bookings on one row are plausible, and 39 rows cannot move the model. The app accepts values up to twice the training maximum
meal = Undefined 1,169 recode as SC (no meal package), as defined in the data paper

What the leakage detectors can and cannot show.

  • The first detector (groups with ≥ 99 % or ≤ 1 % cancellation) looks only at attributes with ≤ 30 levels.
  • The second scores every attribute on its own on later arrivals. It is a screen for strong single-field leaks: only reservation_status stands out (AUC 1.00). It uses raw numeric values, so it only catches monotone patterns, and it cannot see a partial leak hidden inside a genuine field.
  • That partial case is exactly what the within-segment test in 2.3 (finding 4) found for country.

🔍 Critic review — Data Understanding¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on CRISP-DM, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on the CRISP-DM methodology. Review the Data Understanding phase of my hotel-cancellation project below. Check it against every generic task and output CRISP-DM 1.0 defines for this phase. Focus especially on: whether each hypothesis is testable, whether data quality issues are quantified, and whether every attribute was audited for availability at booking time (target leakage). List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Non Refund anomaly noted but not investigated; country may be corrected at check-in (possible leakage). Added a Non Refund profile (97 % Portuguese group/tour-operator blocks); planned a sensitivity test for country (done in 5.2).
2 Leakage audit skipped high-cardinality fields; Non Refund and duplicate hypotheses untested; no timeline drift. Single-attribute AUC screen over every field; NR is 98 % duplicates; duplicate profile; timeline plot; more quality rows.
3 The country defaulting hypothesis was testable but untested; drift comparison confounded by season. Within-segment test: no-shows and cancellations ~95 % Portuguese vs ~25 % of check-outs → country excluded; like-for-like drift.

Output: Rationale for inclusion/exclusion¶

Attributes are excluded for one of three reasons:

  • they encode the outcome: reservation_status, reservation_status_date, and country, which is probably defaulted for guests who never arrived (2.3 finding 4);
  • they are set or updated after booking: assigned_room_type, booking_changes, required_car_parking_spaces;
  • they would not generalise: arrival_date_year, because future bookings have unseen years.

agent and company are kept in their raw form and turned into agent_id and has_company by the score code in 3.3, so the model's input is exactly the 24 raw fields a booking system exports. total_of_special_requests and adr have uncertain recording times. They are kept and labelled as such in the log, and their effect is measured in 5.2. Every other attribute is known at booking time and plausibly related to cancellation (2.3). Rows removed in 3.2 are invalid records (no guests, impossible prices): 182 bookings, 0.15 %.

3.3 Construct data¶

In [14]:
# Construct data AS SCORE CODE: a small module shared by the notebook and the deployed app, so the model can be fed raw
# booking fields straight from a property-management-system export and both apply exactly the same steps.
FEATURE_CODE = r'''
# Score code for the hotel-cancellation model: raw booking fields -> model inputs (Phase 3.3 Construct data).
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

RAW_FIELDS = ["hotel", "lead_time", "arrival_date_month", "arrival_date_week_number", "arrival_date_day_of_month",
              "stays_in_weekend_nights", "stays_in_week_nights", "adults", "children", "babies", "meal",
              "market_segment", "distribution_channel", "is_repeated_guest", "previous_cancellations",
              "previous_bookings_not_canceled", "reserved_room_type", "deposit_type", "agent", "company",
              "days_in_waiting_list", "customer_type", "adr", "total_of_special_requests"]
RAW_CATEGORICAL = ["hotel", "arrival_date_month", "meal", "market_segment", "distribution_channel",
                   "reserved_room_type", "deposit_type", "customer_type"]
NUMERIC = ["lead_time", "arrival_date_week_number", "arrival_date_day_of_month", "stays_in_weekend_nights",
           "stays_in_week_nights", "adults", "children", "babies", "is_repeated_guest", "previous_cancellations",
           "previous_bookings_not_canceled", "days_in_waiting_list", "adr", "total_of_special_requests",
           "total_nights", "total_guests", "has_kids", "has_company"]
CATEGORICAL = RAW_CATEGORICAL + ["agent_id"]


def prepare(raw):
    # Raw booking rows (RAW_FIELDS) -> model inputs. Stateless, so it is safe inside the pipeline.
    d = pd.DataFrame(raw).copy()
    for c in RAW_FIELDS:
        if c not in RAW_CATEGORICAL:
            d[c] = pd.to_numeric(d[c], errors="coerce")        # 'NULL' agent/company ids become missing
    d["children"] = d["children"].fillna(0)                      # 4 bookings: no children recorded
    d["meal"] = d["meal"].replace({"Undefined": "SC"})           # both mean 'no meal package'
    d["total_nights"] = d["stays_in_week_nights"] + d["stays_in_weekend_nights"]
    d["total_guests"] = d["adults"] + d["children"] + d["babies"]
    d["has_kids"] = ((d["children"] + d["babies"]) > 0).astype(int)
    d["agent_id"] = d["agent"].map(lambda a: "none" if pd.isna(a) else str(int(a)))
    d["has_company"] = d["company"].notna().astype(int)
    out = d[NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL].copy()
    out[CATEGORICAL] = out[CATEGORICAL].astype(object).where(out[CATEGORICAL].notna(), np.nan)
    return out


class CalibratedModel:
    # Deployed model: the evaluated pipeline's scores mapped through an isotonic calibration fitted on
    # out-of-fold training predictions, so the output can be read (and summed) as a probability.
    def __init__(self, model, calibrator):
        self.model, self.calibrator = model, calibrator
        self.classes_ = np.array([0, 1])

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        p = np.clip(self.calibrator.predict(self.model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]), 0, 1)
        return np.column_stack([1 - p, p])
'''
(APP / "booking_features.py").write_text(FEATURE_CODE.lstrip(), encoding="utf-8")

Output: Derived attributes¶

The construction step is written as score code, a small module booking_features.py saved next to the app. Its prepare() function is the first step of the model pipeline. The model therefore takes the 24 raw fields a booking system exports and derives everything else itself, and the notebook and the app run exactly the same code.

Attribute Definition Rationale
total_nights, total_guests sums compact summaries of trip size. Their individual effect is not scored separately: 5.1 ranks the raw fields
has_kids children or babies on the booking a simple family-travel flag. No exploration finding tests it; kept because it is cheap and harmless for trees
agent_id travel agent as a category (none if booked without one) agents differ sharply (the 5 largest handle half of all bookings); agent is a top-4 driver in 5.1
has_company a company pays replaces the 94 %-missing company ID (2.4)

Removed in revision 2: arrival_weekday, adr_per_guest, has_agent and room_type_x_hotel. No exploration finding supported them, their permutation importances in the first run were 0.0021 or less, and has_agent duplicated agent_id.

Output: Generated records¶

None. Classes are only moderately imbalanced (≈ 37 % cancelled), so no oversampling.

Output: Merged data¶

Two source tables (resort, city) share one schema but were formatted inconsistently. Each was harmonised (snake_case names, trimmed text, "NULL" → missing, consistent types), given a hotel attribute to preserve provenance, and stacked (a union, not a join — there are no shared keys). 3.5 Format data¶

In [16]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, FunctionTransformer

# Time-based split: train on earlier arrivals, test on the most recent 20 % (mimics real use)
df = df.sort_values("arrival_date", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
cutoff = df["arrival_date"].quantile(1 - TEST_SIZE)
is_test = df["arrival_date"] > cutoff

X = df[RAW_FIELDS]                       # raw booking fields; the pipeline's first step (prepare) builds the model inputs
y = df[TARGET].astype(int)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = X[~is_test], X[is_test], y[~is_test], y[is_test]

num_pipe = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
cat_pipe = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="missing")),
                     ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=0.005,
                                              max_categories=30, sparse_output=False))])
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([("num", num_pipe, NUMERIC), ("cat", cat_pipe, CATEGORICAL)])

dataset_description = pd.DataFrame({
    "set": ["train", "test"], "rows": [len(X_train), len(X_test)],
    "arrivals_from": [df.loc[~is_test, "arrival_date"].min().date(), df.loc[is_test, "arrival_date"].min().date()],
    "arrivals_to": [df.loc[~is_test, "arrival_date"].max().date(), df.loc[is_test, "arrival_date"].max().date()],
    "cancel_rate": [round(y_train.mean(), 3), round(y_test.mean(), 3)]})
dataset_description.to_csv(REP / "dataset_description.csv", index=False)

Output: Reformatted data · Dataset · Dataset description¶

The model takes 24 raw booking fields. The score code turns them into 18 numeric and 9 categorical model inputs (printed above). Numeric inputs are median-imputed and standardised; categorical inputs are one-hot encoded, with categories under 0.5 % of bookings (e.g. rare agents) pooled into an "infrequent" level so the model doesn't memorise them. Construction, imputation and encoding live in one scikit-learn pipeline that is fitted on training data only and saved with the model, so the app applies exactly the same transformations to raw booking-system data.

Some fields are exact sums of others (total_nights = week + weekend nights, total_guests = adults + children + babies). That is harmless for the tree models. For logistic regression the L2 penalty keeps the coefficients identified, but they should not be read one by one.

Time-based split: bookings are ordered by arrival date; the latest 20 % of arrivals (23 April – 31 August 2017, 23,795 bookings, 40.9 % cancelled) form the test set, and everything earlier (1 July 2015 – 22 April 2017, 95,413 bookings, 36.1 % cancelled) is for training. This mimics real use: the model is always applied to bookings that arrive after the data it learned from. Cancellations rose like for like (finding 7), so the test period is harder than the training period. 5.1 also checks a split by booking date, which is closer still to how the app is used.

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

Review the Data Preparation phase of my hotel-cancellation project below. Check it against every generic task and output CRISP-DM 1.0 defines for this phase. Focus especially on: data leakage (both target leakage and train/test contamination), whether every quality issue from Phase 2 was resolved, and whether each derived attribute is justified by an exploration finding. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Keeping 27 % duplicate rows lets identical bookings sit in both training and validation folds. Kept them (no booking ID) but changed the test design to time-series folds (4.2).
2 Booking date derivable; derived features unjustified (importance ≈ 0); folds could split same-day duplicates. Four derived features dropped; construction moved into the pipeline as score code; date-aligned folds; booking-date check.

Phase 4 — Modeling¶

Goal: select and apply modeling techniques and calibrate their parameters.

4.1 Select modeling technique¶

In [17]:
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier

class NonRefundRule(ClassifierMixin, BaseEstimator):
    """What a hotel could do without a model: treat every 'Non Refund' deposit booking as a cancellation."""
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.classes_ = np.array([0, 1]); return self
    def predict_proba(self, X):
        p = (pd.DataFrame(X)["deposit_type"] == "Non Refund").to_numpy(float)
        return np.column_stack([1 - p, p])
    def predict(self, X):
        return (self.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] >= 0.5).astype(int)

BASELINES = {   # benchmarks that use raw fields directly
    "Baseline: majority class": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "Baseline: Non Refund rule": NonRefundRule(),
    "Baseline: lead time only": Pipeline([("pick", ColumnTransformer([("lt", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p), ["lead_time"])])),
                                          ("model", LogisticRegression())]),
}
MODELS = {      # candidate models, each wrapped as prepare -> preprocess -> estimator
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150, min_samples_leaf=5, max_depth=25, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "HistGradientBoosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
}
make_model = lambda est: Pipeline([("construct", FunctionTransformer(prepare)), ("prep", preprocessor), ("model", est)])

Output: Modeling technique¶

  • Baselines: the majority class (predicts "not cancelled" for everyone: the floor), the "Non Refund" rule (flag every Non Refund deposit, which a hotel could do without any model), and lead time only (a one-variable logistic regression). A model is only worth deploying if it clearly beats the rule.
  • Logistic regression: interpretable linear benchmark.
  • Random forest and histogram gradient boosting: tree ensembles that capture interactions such as lead time × deposit type × segment without manual feature engineering.

No class weighting: the imbalance is mild (37 % positives). Probabilities are calibrated after model selection (5.1) and the decision threshold is tuned for business value.

Output: Modeling assumptions¶

Technique Assumptions How addressed
Logistic regression linear effects in log-odds; scaled inputs; no exact collinearity scaling in the pipeline; the exact sums (3.5) are handled by the L2 penalty, and coefficients are not interpreted one by one
Random forest / gradient boosting no distributional assumptions; enough samples per leaf min_samples_leaf ≥ 5 and depth capped — limits memorising duplicate rows and keeps the model small enough to deploy
All the scores are not automatically calibrated probabilities isotonic calibration on out-of-fold training scores; reliability curve and Brier score on test (5.1)
All training and future bookings come from the same process time-ordered validation and test; drift monitoring

4.2 Generate test design¶

In [18]:
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_validate

# X_train is ordered by arrival date (3.5). Each fold trains on EARLIER arrivals and validates on the NEXT block,
# exactly how the model will be used. Fold edges are moved to date boundaries so identical same-day rows
# (27 % of rows are exact duplicates) can never sit on both sides of a fold. Shuffled K-fold was rejected:
# it mixed past and future and over-estimated ROC-AUC (0.956 vs 0.868 on later arrivals, see 4.4).
def date_blocked_folds(dates, n_splits):
    dates = pd.Series(np.asarray(dates))
    starts = [dates.iloc[va[0]] for _, va in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=n_splits).split(dates)]
    ends = starts[1:] + [dates.iloc[-1] + pd.Timedelta(days=1)]
    return [(np.flatnonzero(dates < s), np.flatnonzero((dates >= s) & (dates < e))) for s, e in zip(starts, ends)]

train_dates = df.loc[X_train.index, "arrival_date"].reset_index(drop=True)
CV = date_blocked_folds(train_dates, CV_FOLDS)
SCORING = {"roc_auc": "roc_auc", "precision": "precision", "recall": "recall", "f1": "f1", "accuracy": "accuracy"}
PRIMARY = "roc_auc"
FOLD_NAMES = []
for i, (tr, va) in enumerate(CV, 1):
    FOLD_NAMES.append(f"fold {i}: {train_dates.iloc[va].min():%Y-%m-%d}..{train_dates.iloc[va].max():%Y-%m-%d}")
    print(f"fold {i}: train {train_dates.iloc[tr].min().date()} .. {train_dates.iloc[tr].max().date()} ({len(tr):,})"
          f"  ->  validate {train_dates.iloc[va].min().date()} .. {train_dates.iloc[va].max().date()} ({len(va):,})")

fold 1: train 2015-07-01 .. 2015-10-24 (15,851)  ->  validate 2015-10-25 .. 2016-03-24 (15,936)
fold 2: train 2015-07-01 .. 2016-03-24 (31,787)  ->  validate 2016-03-25 .. 2016-06-21 (15,902)
fold 3: train 2015-07-01 .. 2016-06-21 (47,689)  ->  validate 2016-06-22 .. 2016-09-27 (15,820)
fold 4: train 2015-07-01 .. 2016-09-27 (63,509)  ->  validate 2016-09-28 .. 2017-01-07 (15,898)
fold 5: train 2015-07-01 .. 2017-01-07 (79,407)  ->  validate 2017-01-08 .. 2017-04-22 (16,006)

Output: Test design¶

Model selection uses time-series cross-validation (5 expanding-window folds, printed above) on the training period only: every fold trains on earlier arrivals and validates on later ones, mirroring real use. Fold edges are moved to date boundaries, so the 27 % exact-duplicate rows (mostly multi-room group bookings, 2.3 finding 8) can never sit on both sides of a fold. Shuffled K-fold was rejected because it mixes future bookings into training and puts identical rows on both sides of a fold. That inflated ROC-AUC well above what the model achieves on genuinely new bookings (4.4). Tuning uses the same folds, so tuned and default scores are directly comparable, and per-fold scores are reported so differences can be judged against fold-to-fold noise.

Honest note on the test period: in the first iteration it was scored once and compared with shuffled CV, and that gap (0.956 vs 0.868) led to this design. Its results were also visible during the two later review rounds. Every later change was justified on cross-validation and on data-understanding evidence (for example the nationality test), but the test period is no longer pristine. Cross-validation is therefore reported as primary evidence next to every test result (5.1). Primary metric ROC-AUC (threshold-free ranking quality); precision and recall are evaluated at the business-optimal threshold chosen on training data.

from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
SEARCH_SPACES = {
    "Logistic Regression": {"C": loguniform(1e-3, 1e2)},
    "Random Forest": {"n_estimators": [100, 200], "max_depth": [15, 25, 40], "min_samples_leaf": [5, 10, 20, 50, 100],
                      "max_features": ["sqrt", 0.3]},
    "HistGradientBoosting": {"learning_rate": loguniform(0.03, 0.3), "max_iter": [200, 400, 600],
                             "max_leaf_nodes": [31, 63, 127], "min_samples_leaf": [10, 20, 50, 100],
                             "l2_regularization": loguniform(1e-4, 1.0)},
}
# Every family gets the same random-search budget on the same folds. Tuned settings are adopted only if they beat the
# defaults by more than one standard error of the paired per-fold differences (a best-of-N maximum is optimistic).
tuned, tuning_rows, tuning_logs = {}, [], []
for name, est in MODELS.items():
    search = RandomizedSearchCV(make_model(est), {f"model__{k}": v for k, v in SEARCH_SPACES[name].items()},
                                n_iter=N_TUNING_ITER, cv=CV, scoring=PRIMARY, n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    best_folds = np.array([search.cv_results_[f"split{i}_test_score"][search.best_index_] for i in range(len(CV))])
    diff = best_folds - fold_auc[name]; se = diff.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(diff))
    adopt = diff.mean() > se
    params = {k.replace("model__", ""): (round(v, 5) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in search.best_params_.items()}
    tuned[name] = {"fold_auc": best_folds if adopt else fold_auc[name], "params": params if adopt else "defaults",
                   "estimator": search.best_estimator_ if adopt else make_model(est).fit(X_train, y_train)}
    tuning_rows.append({"model": name, "default_auc": fold_auc[name].mean(), "best_tuned_auc": best_folds.mean(),
                        "gain": diff.mean(), "gain_se": se, "adopted": "tuned" if adopt else "defaults", "settings": str(params)})
    tuning_logs.append(pd.DataFrame(search.cv_results_)[["params", "mean_test_score", "std_test_score"]].assign(model=name))
tuning_table = pd.DataFrame(tuning_rows).set_index("model").round(4)
pd.concat(tuning_logs).sort_values(["model", "mean_test_score"], ascending=[True, False]).to_csv(REP / "tuning_results.csv", index=False)
display(tuning_table)

best_name = max(means, key=means.get)

                        "se": (tuned[best_name]["fold_auc"] - t["fold_auc"]).std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(CV)),
                        "folds_won": f"{int(((tuned[best_name]['fold_auc'] - t['fold_auc']) > 0).sum())}/{len(CV)}"}
                       for other, t in tuned.items() if other != best_name]).round(4)

Output: Parameter settings¶

Every model family got the same tuning budget: 8 random-search candidates on the same five folds. Tuned settings were adopted only if they beat the defaults by more than one standard error of the paired per-fold differences, because the best of 8 noisy scores is optimistic by construction. Eight candidates is a thin budget for the 5-parameter gradient-boosting space, so its ranking could change with a larger search.

Family Default CV ROC-AUC Best tuned Adopted
Random forest 0.844 0.849 (+0.005 ± 0.005) defaults: the gain is within noise
Gradient boosting 0.840 0.834 defaults (tuning did not help)
Logistic regression 0.812 0.816 (+0.004 ± 0.004) defaults: the gain is within noise

Final: random forest with 150 trees, max depth 25, at least 5 bookings per leaf, √p features per split. It beats logistic regression on 5 of 5 folds (+0.033 ± 0.016 AUC) and gradient boosting on 4 of 5 folds (+0.004 ± 0.002). Its lead over boosting is consistent but small. The full tuning log is in artifacts/reports/tuning_results.csv and the paired comparison in champion_paired_comparison.csv.

Output: Models¶

Three baselines, three candidate pipelines (score code + preprocessing + estimator) and their tuned variants.

Output: Model description¶

The approved model averages 150 decision trees. Each is grown on a bootstrap sample of the training bookings, using a random subset of attributes at each split, with at least 5 bookings per leaf. For a new booking, each tree returns the share of cancelled training bookings in the leaf it lands in, and the forest averages these shares. That score ranks bookings but is not a calibrated probability, so 5.1 calibrates it. It relies most on deposit type, special requests, lead time, travel agent and customer type (permutation importance, 5.1).

4.4 Assess model¶

Output: Model assessment¶

Model CV ROC-AUC (mean ± sd) Comment
Random forest 0.844 ± 0.019 best on 4–5 of 5 folds against each rival; adopted
Gradient boosting 0.840 ± 0.021 close second
Logistic regression 0.812 ± 0.034 linear benchmark, clearly behind once nationality is removed
Baseline: lead time only 0.688 the single strongest attribute on its own
Baseline: Non Refund rule 0.664 precision 0.99 but recall only 0.33: it finds one kind of cancellation
Baseline: majority class 0.500 floor

Without nationality, no model reaches the 0.85 ROC-AUC criterion on cross-validation (the random forest comes closest at 0.844). With nationality it was 0.878, and 5.2 shows what that field was worth. All three models beat the best baseline by 0.12–0.16. The hardest block is summer 2016 (fold 3: RF 0.810), and the easiest are spring 2016 and early 2017 (folds 2 and 5: 0.862–0.863), so difficulty varies with the season. min_samples_leaf = 5 keeps the trees from fitting single bookings. It cannot stop a set of dozens of identical duplicate rows from filling a leaf, which is why the folds are cut at date boundaries.

Output: Revised parameter settings¶

  • Iteration 1 → 2: with shuffled 5-fold CV the random forest scored ROC-AUC 0.956, but only 0.868 on the later test period. The test design was changed to date-aligned time-series folds.
  • Iteration 2 → 3: three baselines, an equal tuning budget and a one-standard-error adoption rule were added; the defaults were kept.
  • Iteration 3 → 4: country was removed after the defaulting test (2.3). CV ROC-AUC fell from 0.878 to 0.844.

🔍 Critic review — Modeling¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on CRISP-DM, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on the CRISP-DM methodology. Review the Modeling phase of my hotel-cancellation project below. Check it against every generic task and output CRISP-DM 1.0 defines for this phase. Focus especially on: whether the baseline and benchmark comparisons are meaningful, whether the test design prevents optimistic bias (time-based hold-out, no tuning on test), whether the search space is sensible, and whether model assumptions were checked. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Shuffled CV gave 0.956 vs 0.868 on the later test period; tuned settings did not beat the defaults. Time-series CV (now 0.877 vs 0.868); tuning adopted only if it beats defaults on the same folds.
2 Three figures corrupted by a plotting bug; test period informed the redesign; no rule baseline; unequal tuning. Figures fixed; Non Refund and lead-time baselines; equal tuning with a 1-SE adoption rule; paired per-fold comparison; disclosure.
3 Test results visible during every revision; calibrator fitted on weaker fold models; thin search budget for boosting. CV reported as primary evidence; calibrator on folds 3–5; budget limit acknowledged. Without country: CV AUC 0.844.

Phase 5 — Evaluation¶

Goal: judge the model against the business objectives, review the process, and decide the next steps.

5.1 Evaluate results¶

from sklearn import metrics as M
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression

# 1) Out-of-fold scores for every training validation block (training data only)
def oof_scores(model):
    s = np.full(len(y_train), np.nan)
    for tr, va in CV:
        s[va] = clone(model).fit(X_train.iloc[tr], y_train.iloc[tr]).predict_proba(X_train.iloc[va])[:, 1]
    return s
oof = oof_scores(best_model)
has = ~np.isnan(oof); y_oof, oof_raw = y_train.to_numpy()[has], oof[has]

# 2) Calibrate: isotonic map from score to observed cancellation rate, fitted on the training OOF scores only
late = np.zeros(len(y_train), bool); late[np.concatenate([va for _, va in CV[2:]])] = True; late = late[has]
calibrator = IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds="clip", y_min=0, y_max=1).fit(oof_raw[late], y_oof[late])   # folds 3-5: models trained on 48k-79k bookings
oof_cal = calibrator.predict(oof_raw)
deployed_model = CalibratedModel(best_model, calibrator)

# 3) Choose the decision threshold on the calibrated training OOF scores, maximising business value
def net_value(y_true, p, t, cost_fp=COST_FP, value_tp=VALUE_TP):
    yp = p >= t; yt = np.asarray(y_true) == 1
    return (yp & yt).sum() * value_tp - (yp & ~yt).sum() * cost_fp - (~yp & yt).sum() * COST_FN
grid = np.round(np.arange(0.05, 0.96, 0.01), 2)
train_value = np.array([net_value(y_oof, oof_cal, t) for t in grid])
DECISION_THRESHOLD = float(grid[train_value.argmax()])
oof_flag = oof_cal >= DECISION_THRESHOLD
print(f"Decision threshold (calibrated probability, chosen on training OOF): {DECISION_THRESHOLD:.2f} | "
      f"training OOF precision {M.precision_score(y_oof, oof_flag):.3f}, recall {M.recall_score(y_oof, oof_flag):.3f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(grid, train_value / len(y_oof) * 1000, c="#4C72B0"); ax.axvline(DECISION_THRESHOLD, c="r", ls="--", label=f"chosen {DECISION_THRESHOLD:.2f}")
ax.axhline(0, c="gray", lw=.8); ax.legend()
ax.set(title="Net value per 1,000 bookings vs. threshold (training OOF, calibrated scores)", xlabel="decision threshold", ylabel="EUR")
savefig("eval_threshold_selection")

# 4) Evaluate on the held-out test period (ROC-AUC on the raw ranking scores; flags on calibrated probabilities)
proba_raw = best_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
proba = calibrator.predict(proba_raw)
pred = (proba >= DECISION_THRESHOLD).astype(int)
test_metrics = {"roc_auc": M.roc_auc_score(y_test, proba_raw), "pr_auc": M.average_precision_score(y_test, proba_raw),
                "precision": M.precision_score(y_test, pred), "recall": M.recall_score(y_test, pred),
                "f1": M.f1_score(y_test, pred), "accuracy": M.accuracy_score(y_test, pred),
                "brier_raw": M.brier_score_loss(y_test, proba_raw), "brier_calibrated": M.brier_score_loss(y_test, proba)}

# 95 % confidence intervals: block bootstrap over arrival weeks (bookings in the same week are not independent)
weeks = df.loc[X_test.index, "arrival_date"].dt.to_period("W").to_numpy()
week_rows = {w: np.flatnonzero(weeks == w) for w in np.unique(weeks)}
rng, yt_all, boots = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE), y_test.to_numpy(), []
for _ in range(300):
    ix = np.concatenate([week_rows[w] for w in rng.choice(list(week_rows), len(week_rows))])
    boots.append({"roc_auc": M.roc_auc_score(yt_all[ix], proba_raw[ix]), "precision": M.precision_score(yt_all[ix], pred[ix]),
                  "recall": M.recall_score(yt_all[ix], pred[ix])})
ci = pd.DataFrame(boots).quantile([0.025, 0.975])
crit = pd.DataFrame([{"criterion": m, "threshold": t, "test_value": round(test_metrics[m], 4),
                      "ci_95_low": round(ci.loc[0.025, m], 4), "ci_95_high": round(ci.loc[0.975, m], 4),
                      "met": test_metrics[m] >= t, "met_at_ci_low": ci.loc[0.025, m] >= t} for m, t in SUCCESS_CRITERIA.items()])
crit.to_csv(REP / "success_criteria_assessment.csv", index=False)

# Business impact on the test period.
# (a) Per booking: what each flagging strategy is worth under the cost model (threshold decisions).
per_k = lambda v: v / len(y_test) * 1000
nr_flag = (X_test["deposit_type"] == "Non Refund").to_numpy()
lr_model = tuned["Logistic Regression"]["estimator"]

              "Rule: flag Non Refund deposits": nr_flag, f"Logistic regression (threshold {lr_t:.2f})": lr_proba >= lr_t,
              f"{best_name}, threshold 0.50": proba >= 0.5, f"{best_name}, threshold {DECISION_THRESHOLD:.2f}": pred.astype(bool)}

                          "bookings_flagged_%": f.mean() * 100, "precision": M.precision_score(y_test, f, zero_division=0),

# Sensitivity to the cost assumption (wrong-flag cost / right-flag value); threshold re-chosen on training OOF each time
sens = []
for ratio in [0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4]:
    cfp = ratio * VALUE_TP
    t = float(grid[np.argmax([net_value(y_oof, oof_cal, g, cost_fp=cfp) for g in grid])])
    f = proba >= t
    sens.append({"cost_FP / value_TP": ratio, "threshold": t, "model_eur_per_1000": per_k(net_value(y_test, proba, t, cost_fp=cfp)),
                 "non_refund_rule_eur_per_1000": per_k(net_value(y_test, nr_flag.astype(float), 0.5, cost_fp=cfp)),
                 "flagged_%": f.mean() * 100, "precision": M.precision_score(y_test, f), "recall": M.recall_score(y_test, f)})
cost_sensitivity = pd.DataFrame(sens).round(3); cost_sensitivity.to_csv(REP / "cost_sensitivity.csv", index=False)
display(cost_sensitivity)

# (b) Per NIGHT: the real decision is how many extra rooms to sell for each arrival date. Missed cancellations and
# false flags on the same night offset each other, so the value is simulated per hotel x arrival date:
#   re-sold rooms = min(allowance, actual cancellations); walked guests = max(0, allowance - actual cancellations),
#   both on a full night only (x P_FULL). The INCUMBENT is the hotel's rule of thumb: the historical cancellation rate
#   of that hotel and arrival month (training period) x bookings on the books.
t_df = df.loc[X_test.index, ["hotel", "arrival_date"]].assign(y=y_test.to_numpy(), p=proba, flag=pred, nr=nr_flag.astype(int))
hist = df.loc[~is_test].groupby(["hotel", df.loc[~is_test, "arrival_date"].dt.month])[TARGET].mean()
t_df["hist"] = [hist.get((h, m), y_train.mean()) for h, m in zip(t_df["hotel"], t_df["arrival_date"].dt.month)]
nights = t_df.groupby(["hotel", "arrival_date"]).agg(bookings=("y", "size"), cancels=("y", "sum"), sum_p=("p", "sum"),
                                                     flags=("flag", "sum"), nr=("nr", "sum"), hist=("hist", "sum")).reset_index()
night_value = lambda allow, c: P_FULL * (RESALE_VALUE * np.minimum(allow, c) - WALK_COST * np.maximum(allow - c, 0))
POLICIES = {"No overbooking": lambda n: np.zeros(len(n)),
            "Incumbent: historical rate x bookings": lambda n: np.round(n["hist"]),
            "Rule: count Non Refund bookings": lambda n: n["nr"],
            f"Model: count flagged bookings (p >= {DECISION_THRESHOLD:.2f})": lambda n: n["flags"],
            "Model: sum of probabilities (expected cancellations)": lambda n: np.round(n["sum_p"])}
for name, pol in POLICIES.items():
    nights[name] = night_value(pol(nights), nights["cancels"])
weeks_n = nights["arrival_date"].dt.to_period("W").astype(str).to_numpy()
n_weeks = len(np.unique(weeks_n))
boot_idx = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_STATE).integers(0, n_weeks, (500, n_weeks))     # block bootstrap over arrival weeks
def boot_ci(col):
    s = nights.groupby(weeks_n)[[col, "bookings"]].sum()
    a, b = s[col].to_numpy()[boot_idx].sum(1), s["bookings"].to_numpy()[boot_idx].sum(1)
    return np.quantile(a / b * 1000, [.025, .975])
inc = "Incumbent: historical rate x bookings"
per_night = []
for name, pol in POLICIES.items():
    allow = pol(nights)
    nights[f"diff_{name}"] = nights[name] - nights[inc]
    lo, hi = boot_ci(f"diff_{name}") if name != inc else (0.0, 0.0)
    per_night.append({"policy": name, "eur_per_1000_bookings": nights[name].sum() / nights["bookings"].sum() * 1000,
                      "vs_incumbent": nights[f"diff_{name}"].sum() / nights["bookings"].sum() * 1000, "vs_incumbent_ci_low": lo, "vs_incumbent_ci_high": hi,
                      "mean_abs_error_rooms_per_night": np.mean(np.abs(allow - nights["cancels"])), "walk_nights_%": np.mean(allow > nights["cancels"]) * 100})
per_night = pd.DataFrame(per_night).set_index("policy").round(1)
per_night.to_csv(REP / "business_impact_per_night.csv"); display(per_night)
print(f"{len(nights):,} hotel-nights in the test period; mean {nights['cancels'].mean():.1f} cancellations per arrival date")
print("Note: April-August is high season (test cancel rate 40.9 % vs 36.1 % in training), so these are high-season values.")

262 hotel-nights in the test period; mean 37.1 cancellations per arrival date
Note: April-August is high season (test cancel rate 40.9 % vs 36.1 % in training), so these are high-season values.

Output: Assessment of data mining results w.r.t. business success criteria¶

Calibration. The isotonic calibration is fitted on the out-of-fold scores of folds 3–5. Those fold models are trained on 48k–79k bookings, the closest in size to the final model. The test Brier score improves from 0.168 to 0.163. The reliability curve moves towards the diagonal, but at the top end the model still over-states risk somewhat, so the monitoring plan re-checks calibration (6.2).

Data mining criteria — one of three met. Threshold 0.67 is the cost-optimal threshold on training data under the 2 : 1 cost ratio of 1.2.

Criterion Target Cross-validation (primary) Test Test 95 % CI Met
ROC-AUC ≥ 0.85 0.841 0.827 0.810 – 0.846 no
Precision at 0.67 ≥ 0.75 0.949 0.831 0.797 – 0.858 yes, including the CI's lower end
Recall at 0.67 ≥ 0.50 0.405 0.471 0.422 – 0.525 no

The confusion matrix: 4,581 cancellations caught, 5,145 missed, 928 false alarms among 14,069 bookings that arrived. As a per-booking classifier the model does not meet its goals, so it is not approved for acting on individual bookings.

Business criteria — the overbooking forecast. The real decision is per night: how many extra rooms to sell. Missed cancellations and wrong flags on the same night cancel out. So each policy was simulated per hotel × arrival date on the test period (262 hotel-nights, on average 37 cancellations per date): a re-sold room or a walked guest counts only on a full night (× 50 %).

Overbooking policy (per 1,000 bookings) Net value vs. current rule (95 % CI) Average error, rooms per night
No overbooking €0 −€13,429 37.1
Current rule of thumb (historical rate of that hotel and month × bookings) €13,429 — 9.4
Count Non Refund bookings €4,814 −€8,615 28.4
Count the model's flagged bookings €11,538 −€1,891 (−3,108 to −683) 16.1
Model: expected cancellations (sum of probabilities) €16,804 +€3,375 (+2,445 to +4,324) 4.6
  • Revenue recovered: met. Adding up the calibrated probabilities beats the hotel's current rule by about €3,400 per 1,000 bookings, and the whole confidence interval is above zero. At ~55,000 bookings a year that is roughly €190,000 a year for the two hotels, at high-season rates (the test period is April–August).
  • Forecast accuracy: met. It misses the true number of cancellations by 4.6 rooms per night against 9.4 for the current rule. It errs on the high side on 43 % of nights (the current rule on 39 %).
  • Counting flagged bookings is worse than the current rule: flags miss most cancellations (recall 0.47), so the per-booking threshold is the wrong tool for this decision.
  • Actionability: 83 % of flagged bookings really cancel, but outside the Non Refund blocks it is 71 % (below), so the watch list is information only.
  • Usability: not yet verified. The app works (Phase 6), but the staff test belongs to the pilot.

The per-booking money view, with the threshold and cost-ratio sensitivity, is in business_impact.csv and cost_sensitivity.csv. At the assumed 2 : 1 ratio the model is worth €5,700 per 1,000 bookings against €4,800 for the Non Refund rule and logistic regression.

Robustness:

  • Without the Non Refund blocks (a suspected data artefact): AUC 0.774, precision 0.71, recall 0.31. Much of the per-booking signal is the Non Refund block itself.
  • By hotel: AUC 0.837 (city) and 0.805 (resort). The resort's recall is only 0.22 at this threshold.
  • By booking date: for test bookings made after the training cut-off, AUC is 0.760 vs 0.840 for those made before. Compared within lead-time bands, the gap remains (31–90 days: 0.687 vs 0.789; 8–30 days: 0.715 vs 0.730). New bookings really are harder, beyond their shorter lead times.

Drivers (permutation importance on raw booking fields): deposit type (0.093 AUC), special requests (0.054), lead time (0.039), travel agent (0.038) and customer type (0.036), then market segment. This matches the exploration hypotheses (2.3): early, agent- or group-booked, request-free bookings are the risky ones.

Output: Approved models¶

Approved for one use: the random forest (150 trees, depth 25, ≥ 5 per leaf) + isotonic calibration, used to compute each night's expected cancellations (the sum of probabilities) for an internal, randomised overbooking pilot. Not approved for actions on individual bookings, because the per-booking criteria are not met. Bookings above 0.67 appear as an information-only watch list.

# Sensitivity test for attributes that may not be (reliably) known at booking time, and for the two drivers with
# data-quality questions. Uses ONLY the training period - train on everything before the last time-series block,
# evaluate on that block - so the test period is not involved. Each variant gets its own value-optimal threshold
# on the block (optimistic for every variant alike, so the comparison is like for like).
tr_idx, va_idx = CV[-1]
FA, FB = prepare(X_train.iloc[tr_idx]), prepare(X_train.iloc[va_idx])
ya, yb = y_train.iloc[tr_idx], y_train.iloc[va_idx]
champion_est = best_model.named_steps["model"]

def evaluate_variant(drop=(), add=()):
    A = FA.drop(columns=list(drop)).join(df.loc[FA.index, list(add)])
    B = FB.drop(columns=list(drop)).join(df.loc[FB.index, list(add)])
    num = [c for c in NUMERIC if c not in drop] + [a for a in add if df[a].dtype.kind in "if"]
    cat = [c for c in CATEGORICAL if c not in drop] + [a for a in add if df[a].dtype.kind not in "if"]
    prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", clone(num_pipe), num), ("cat", clone(cat_pipe), cat)])
    p = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("model", clone(champion_est))]).fit(A, ya).predict_proba(B)[:, 1]
    values = np.array([net_value(yb, p, t) for t in grid]); t = grid[values.argmax()]
    return {"roc_auc": M.roc_auc_score(yb, p), "threshold": t, "precision": M.precision_score(yb, p >= t),
            "recall": M.recall_score(yb, p >= t), "eur_per_1000": values.max() / len(yb) * 1000}

variants = {"approved attribute set": {}, "+ country (excluded: probable leakage)": {"add": ["country"]},
            "without total_of_special_requests": {"drop": ["total_of_special_requests"]},

            "without deposit_type": {"drop": ["deposit_type"]}, "without adr": {"drop": ["adr"]},

            "+ booking_changes (excluded)": {"add": ["booking_changes"]}}
sensitivity = pd.DataFrame({name: evaluate_variant(**kw) for name, kw in variants.items()}).T.astype(float).round(4)
sensitivity["delta_auc"] = (sensitivity["roc_auc"] - sensitivity.loc["approved attribute set", "roc_auc"]).round(4)
sensitivity["meets_auc_and_precision"] = (sensitivity["roc_auc"] >= SUCCESS_CRITERIA["roc_auc"]) & (sensitivity["precision"] >= SUCCESS_CRITERIA["precision"])
sensitivity.to_csv(REP / "leakage_sensitivity.csv")

5.2 Review process¶

Output: Review of process¶

Leakage sensitivity (table above). This was done on the last training-period block (Jan–Apr 2017), with each variant given its own value-optimal threshold on that block. The thresholds are fitted on the block itself, so the precision values are optimistic for every variant alike and are only for comparison.

  • The approved set (no nationality) scores ROC-AUC 0.863 on this block.
  • Adding back country raises it by +0.034. That is how much the probably-defaulted field was worth, and it matches the drop seen in CV.
  • Adding back the parking attribute adds +0.011, and booking_changes +0.005. Excluding them costs little, so those decisions stand.
  • Removing deposit type costs 0.031; removing special requests 0.021; removing agent and special requests together 0.031. Removing ADR changes nothing.
Phase What went well What was missed / should be redone
Business Understanding one decision (the nightly overbooking level), priced consistently, with the hotel's current rule as benchmark; legal constraint recorded costs, demand and recording practices are assumptions, because no hotel contact was available; the recall floor was added after first results
Data Understanding two leakage detectors; a within-segment test that found the nationality defaulting; Non Refund and duplicate profiles; like-for-like drift the Non Refund meaning still needs the hotel
Data Preparation integration validated against the published file; construction as score code inside the pipeline duplicates kept without a booking ID to prove they are separate rooms (the profile strongly suggests they are)
Modeling three baselines; equal tuning budgets; date-aligned time-ordered folds; paired per-fold comparison 8 candidates is a thin budget for gradient boosting; the test period was visible during revisions
Evaluation per-night simulation against the current rule with bootstrap CIs; calibrated probabilities; results with and without Non Refund, per hotel and per booking-date band the per-booking criteria are not met; new short-notice bookings are much harder

Quality assurance — every use of the test period:

  1. iteration 1 compared it with shuffled CV and triggered the test-design change;
  2. its results were visible during review rounds 2 and 3, and changes were justified on CV and data-understanding evidence;
  3. the evaluation in 5.1;
  4. permutation importance (5.1) and the drift demonstration (6.2), which interpret the model and choose nothing.

Model, tuning, calibration and threshold all come from the training period, and the sensitivity test above used only the training period.

5.3 Determine next steps¶

Output: List of possible actions¶

  1. Deploy the expected-cancellations forecast as an internal, randomised overbooking pilot.
  2. Before go-live:
    • confirm with the hotel when country is recorded, which would confirm the reason it was excluded;
    • confirm what Non Refund deposits mean;
    • confirm the real walk cost and how often the hotels sell out (P_FULL).
  3. Iterate:
    • retrain on the hotel's recent data (2015–17 behaviour may be outdated);
    • add price history and customer history, and per-night capacity data;
    • build a separate model for short-notice bookings;
    • give gradient boosting a larger search budget.
  4. Investigate the Non Refund anomaly as a data-quality project with the hotel.

Output: Decision¶

Deploy (action 1) as a pilot, with action 2 as a go-live condition. Do not use the per-booking flags for decisions. The model misses its per-booking criteria once the leaking nationality field is removed, and that result is reported, not hidden. But the decision the business actually needs, the nightly overbooking level, is clearly better than today's rule. Its confidence interval is above zero, and its error is half the current rule's.

🔍 Critic review — Evaluation¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on CRISP-DM, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on the CRISP-DM methodology. Review the Evaluation phase of my hotel-cancellation project below. Check it against every generic task and output CRISP-DM 1.0 defines for this phase. Focus especially on: whether results are tied back to the business success criteria in money terms, whether the threshold was chosen without looking at the test period, whether performance holds for both hotels, and whether the next-step decision is justified. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Leakage risk of ambiguous attributes not quantified; resort recall much lower than city. Added leakage sensitivity test on the training period (country −0.035 AUC); conditional approval; hotel-specific thresholds listed as next step.
2 Threshold 0.34 under symmetric costs = uncalibrated scores; € compared with straw men; no CIs. Isotonic calibration; Non Refund rule and LR in the € table; block-bootstrap CIs; cost sensitivity; Non Refund-free check.
3 Per-booking pricing ignores that the decision is per night; precision depends on the Non Refund blocks; subgroup failures. Per-night simulation vs the current rule: +€3,375 / 1,000 bookings (CI +2,445 to +4,324). Per-booking criteria reported as not met → only the nightly forecast is approved.

def psi(expected, actual, bins=10):
    """Population Stability Index for a numeric attribute: < 0.1 stable · 0.1–0.25 moderate shift · > 0.25 significant drift."""
    e, a = pd.Series(expected).dropna(), pd.Series(actual).dropna()
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(e, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)))
    if len(edges) < 3: return 0.0
    pe = np.histogram(e, edges)[0] / len(e) + 1e-6
    pa = np.histogram(a.clip(edges[0], edges[-1]), edges)[0] / len(a) + 1e-6
    return float(np.sum((pa - pe) * np.log(pa / pe)))

def psi_categorical(expected, actual, top=20):
    """PSI over category shares (rare categories pooled), for the categorical drivers."""
    keep = pd.Series(expected).value_counts().index[:top]
    pool = lambda s: pd.Series(s).astype(str).where(pd.Series(s).isin(keep), "other").value_counts(normalize=True)
    pe, pa = pool(expected), pool(actual)
    pe, pa = pe.align(pa, fill_value=0)
    return float(np.sum((pa + 1e-6 - pe - 1e-6) * np.log((pa + 1e-6) / (pe + 1e-6))))

# Demonstration: treat the test period as "new production data" and compare it with the training period
F_train, F_test = prepare(X_train), prepare(X_test)
drift = pd.concat([pd.Series({c: psi(F_train[c], F_test[c]) for c in NUMERIC}),
                   pd.Series({c: psi_categorical(F_train[c], F_test[c]) for c in CATEGORICAL})]).round(4).sort_values(ascending=False)
pred_drift = psi(oof_cal, proba)
drift.to_csv(REP / "drift_check_psi.csv")
print(f"Prediction-score PSI (training OOF vs test period): {pred_drift:.3f}"); print(drift.head(12).to_string())
seen_agents = set(F_train["agent_id"]); new_agent = ~F_test["agent_id"].isin(seen_agents)
print(f"Agent drift check (no outcomes needed): {new_agent.mean():.1%} of test-period bookings come from agents never seen in training "
      f"(they are scored through the pooled 'infrequent' agent level)")
