Output: Monitoring and maintenance plan¶

Reading the drift demo above:

  • Score drift. The prediction-score PSI between the training OOF scores and the test period is 0.118, a moderate shift that is consistent with the higher cancellation rate in spring–summer 2017 (finding 7). It already exceeds the 0.1 trigger below. The response must not need outcomes, which arrive only after the stay. So the response is: compare the predicted expected cancellations per night with the current rule's number, and once a month's outcomes are in, re-fit the calibrator on the latest three months.
  • Seasonal attributes. arrival_date_month (PSI 7.9), arrival_date_week_number (7.7) and adr (0.94) look severely "drifted" only because the test period covers April–August while training covers all seasons.
  • Agent mix. It shows real drift (PSI 0.43). The response, again without outcomes: only 1.1 % of test bookings come from agents never seen in training, and those are scored through the pooled "infrequent" agent level. So the drift is a change of mix among known agents, which the model already covers. It is a reason to retrain on schedule, not an emergency.
  • In production, compare each month with the same month of the previous year, and treat the prediction-score PSI as the main alarm.
Monitor Metric Trigger Frequency Action
Input drift PSI per attribute (numeric and categorical: agent, deposit type, segment, …) vs. same month last year PSI > 0.25 monthly check for unseen categories; retrain if persistent
Score drift PSI of predicted probabilities PSI > 0.1 monthly compare forecast with the current rule; re-fit the calibrator once outcomes arrive
Forecast accuracy error of expected vs actual cancellations per night, by arrival month (outcomes are known by the end of the stay, so month M is evaluated early in month M + 1) the forecast's error exceeds the current rule's over a rolling 3 months monthly retrain on the most recent 24 months
Business KPI net value per 1,000 bookings; number of walked guests (pilot arms compared) negative value or rising walks over a rolling quarter quarterly revisit costs and P_FULL (Phase 1)

Ownership and maintenance:

  • The revenue manager owns the model.
  • For each retraining, the analyst re-runs this notebook on fresh data. The notebook is the retraining procedure, so threshold and calibration are re-derived every time.
  • Models are saved as model_v<date>.joblib with their metadata (data window, metrics, hyperparameters, library versions). The previous version is kept for rollback.
  • Retire the model if a retrained version no longer beats the current rule per night, or if booking channels change fundamentally.

6.3 Produce final report¶

Output: Final report¶

This executed notebook is the full technical report (exported as HTML/PDF in report/). Executive summary:

  • Problem: 37 % of bookings at two Portuguese hotels are cancelled. The hotels overbook by a fixed historical rate and have no per-booking risk estimate.
  • Approach: CRISP-DM end to end on 119,208 bookings. Inputs are 24 fields on the booking record. Nationality was removed after a test showed it was probably filled in by default for guests who never arrived. The model was validated on the most recent arrivals.
  • Result:
    • Added up per night, the model's calibrated probabilities forecast cancellations with half the error of the current rule (4.6 vs 9.4 rooms per night).
    • Under the assumed costs that is worth about €3,400 more per 1,000 bookings (95 % CI €2,400–€4,300).
    • As a per-booking classifier it misses its targets (ROC-AUC 0.83 vs 0.85; recall 0.47 vs 0.50), so individual flags are information only.
  • Drivers: deposit type, special requests, lead time, travel agent, customer type.
  • Caveats:
    • costs, demand and recording practices are assumptions;
    • new short-notice bookings are harder;
    • much of the per-booking signal comes from the anomalous Non Refund blocks;
    • the test period was visible during revisions;
    • 2015–17 behaviour may be outdated.
  • Next steps: a randomised overbooking pilot in the city hotel; confirm data-recording practices and costs; retrain on recent data.

Output: Final presentation¶

The Medium article (article/) and the video walkthrough (video/) present the project as problem → data → approach → results (€ impact) → live app → next steps.

6.4 Review project¶

Output: Experience documentation¶

Topic Lesson
Methodology CRISP-DM's insistence on the business decision changed the answer twice. Pricing the decision consistently and per night showed that the per-booking flags are the wrong tool, while the summed probabilities clearly beat the hotel's current rule. A per-booking accuracy table alone would have hidden both.
Leakage The most predictive field was the least trustworthy. A simple within-segment comparison of no-shows, cancellations and check-outs showed nationality was probably defaulted for guests who never arrived. Removing it cost 0.034 AUC and two of three model criteria. That was the right trade.
Validation Shuffled cross-validation was badly optimistic (0.956 vs 0.868 on future bookings). With duplicates and time drift, validation must mimic real use. Splitting the test period by booking date, within lead-time bands, showed a second gap for new bookings.
Probabilities An optimal threshold far from 0.5 under symmetric costs was a symptom of uncalibrated scores. Calibration also made the per-night sum of probabilities usable as a forecast.
Tools / AI assistance AI-generated code ran but needed checking: the first version was too slow and ran out of memory on Colab. Independent AI critics, run in fresh sessions over three rounds, caught the over-optimistic validation, corrupted figures, a one-sided cost model, the missing incumbent benchmark and the untested nationality leak.

🔍 Critic review — Deployment¶

Each phase was reviewed in three rounds with the expert-critic prompt below. Round 1 was run in the drafting session. Rounds 2 and 3 were run by fresh, independent Claude sessions that saw only the executed notebook, its figures and the app files. Full reviews and point-by-point responses: critiques/round_1.md, round_2.md, round_3.md.

You are a world-renowned authority on CRISP-DM, a sought-after keynote speaker, and the author of several award-winning books on the CRISP-DM methodology. Review the Deployment phase of my hotel-cancellation project below. Check it against every generic task and output CRISP-DM 1.0 defines for this phase. Focus especially on: whether the deployment plan is realistic for hotel staff, whether monitoring has concrete triggers, owners and actions, and whether the final report lets a stakeholder act on the results. List (1) anything missing, (2) anything weak or unjustified, (3) methodological errors, and (4) concrete fixes, ranked by importance. Grade it as strictly as you would a professional engagement.

Round Main critique points What I changed
1 Drift demo flags seasonal attributes as drifted, which would cause false alarms. Monitoring now compares same month year-on-year; prediction-score PSI is the main alarm; owner and retraining procedure defined.
2 App needed 32 derived inputs; deployed model ≠ evaluated model; categorical drivers not monitored. App takes raw booking fields; deployed = evaluated model + calibrator; categorical PSI; randomised pilot.
3 Overbooking number ambiguous (flags vs sum of probabilities); alarms without workable responses; trigger fires on noise. One rule (sum of probabilities per date) shown per hotel and date; alarm responses need no outcomes; rolling 3-month trigger.
